Allergic rhinitis

A 2026 randomized comparison found symptom improvement with red-light phototherapy and intranasal steroids, but no difference in biopsy inflammation and larger effects on several symptoms with steroids. Earlier sham-controlled PBM trials reported short-term symptom or airflow improvement; none establishes durable disease control.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A 2026 randomized comparison found symptom improvement with red-light phototherapy and intranasal steroids, but no difference in biopsy inflammation and larger effects on several symptoms with steroids. Earlier sham-controlled PBM trials reported short-term symptom or airflow improvement; none establishes durable disease control.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact Respiratory system > Allergic rhinitis category contains 42 unique titles: 30 human reports, seven animal studies, three meta-analyses, one narrative review, and one protocol. Human reports comprise 17 randomized trials, ten other controlled or single-arm studies, two case reports, and one case series. Reviews reuse primary studies. Records mix red or near-infrared PBM with ultraviolet-containing rhinophototherapy, so they do not represent one intervention.

Human and clinical evidence

A double-blind sham-controlled trial randomized 62 adults; 33 received PBM and 29 sham. After eight sessions over one month, the authors reported better peak nasal inspiratory flow and nasal symptom-control scores, but no significant smell-identification change (Oliveira et al. 2025). In a 2021 placebo-controlled study, 41 of 67 randomized adults completed follow-up; active treatment improved symptom and quality-of-life scores versus sham (Jung et al. 2021). An 80-person randomized study found intranasal laser noninferior to acupuncture, not superior (Kang et al. 2022). Ramasamy et al. randomized 35 people to red-light phototherapy or intranasal corticosteroids for two weeks. Biopsy inflammatory-cell counts and mucosal injury did not differ; symptoms improved in both groups, with larger effects on several subscales in the steroid group, and nasal airflow improved in both (2026). The active-comparator result does not establish superiority over standard medication.

Animal evidence

Seven animal records include four mouse, one rat, and two rabbit studies. Mouse models report reduced allergic symptoms, IgE, eosinophils, or inflammatory markers after selected local-light protocols. A microneedle-delivered 670, 780, 850, or 910 nm protocol reduced allergic features in mice (Ventura et al. 2024). These induced models do not establish patient benefit.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo publication was identified in the exact category.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

Protocols include intranasal red and near-infrared devices, mixed ultraviolet-visible light, different routes, and different schedules. The 2025 sham trial reported 6 J intranasally plus 1 J externally over the nose twice weekly for a month; its abstract does not give exact wavelengths. The 2021 trial used 670 and 830 nm twice daily for four weeks. Other records include 650 nm devices and ultraviolet-containing systems. The treatments and doses are not interchangeable.

Interpretation

Direct trials support a possible short-term symptom benefit for selected PBM protocols, but the 2026 active comparison did not show an advantage over intranasal steroids, and durable control or olfactory benefit remains unestablished. Ultraviolet-containing rhinophototherapy should not be treated as equivalent evidence for red or near-infrared PBM.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow-to-moderate for short-term nasal symptom relief with selected red and near-infrared protocols Very low for durable control, olfactory benefit, and transfer from ultraviolet-containing rhinophototherapy

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

Two sham-controlled trials reported short-term symptom signals, while a recent active-comparator study found red-light phototherapy did not outperform intranasal corticosteroid treatment. Small samples, attrition, mixed spectra, and short follow-up limit certainty. Larger trials should separate conventional red and near-infrared PBM from ultraviolet rhinophototherapy and assess symptoms, airflow, smell, and recurrence over months.
